Surah al-Ikhlas is Meccan and has four verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge.﴾ ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten.﴾ ﴿And there is none comparable to Him.﴾

Al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge): it is fa'al in the sense of maf'ul, from samada ilayhi, meaning he turned to him intending him, and he is the master to whom one turns in needs and who alone suffices for them. The poet said:

Has the messenger of ill news come in the morning with the best of the Banu Asad, with 'Amr ibn Mas'ud, the master, the Samad?

Another said:

I struck him with a sword, then I said to him: "Take it, you are disgraced, for you are the master, the Samad."

Al-kufu (the equal): the peer.

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge.﴾ ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten.﴾ ﴿And there is none comparable to Him.﴾ This surah is Meccan according to the opinion of 'Abd Allah, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, 'Ata', Mujahid and Qatadah, and Madinan according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak.

Since what preceded it mentioned the enmity of the nearest of people to the Messenger (ﷺ), namely his uncle Abu Lahab, and what he suffered from the worshippers of idols who took other gods along with Allah, this surah came expressly affirming Tawhid (the oneness of God), refuting the idol-worshippers, those who said in dualism and trinitarianism and other doctrines opposed to Tawhid. (p-528)

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Jews said: "O Muhammad, describe your Lord to us and give us His lineage," so this was revealed. And it is narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah that the leaders of the factions said: "Give us the lineage of your Lord," so this was revealed. If this cause is authentic, then the pronoun (huwa) refers to the Lord, i.e. ﴿Say: He is Allah﴾, meaning my Lord is Allah, and it is a subject and predicate, with "Ahad" as a second predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ahad" is a substitute for "Allah" or (it is) "huwa ahad." End of quote. If the cause is not authentic, then huwa is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), the matter is the subject, and the sentence after it is a subject and predicate in the position of the predicate of huwa. "Ahad" here means "wahid" (one), i.e. singular in every aspect of unity, meaning in His essence and attributes, not divisible. The hamza of this "ahad" is substituted from a waw, and substituting an open hamza for a waw is rare; from this is the phrase "imra'ah anah" meaning "wanah," because it derives from al-wany, which is weakness, just as "ahad" derives from al-wahda (unity).

Tha'lab said: there is a difference between wahid and ahad. The wahid admits counting, plurality and the dual, while the ahad does not admit them. One says "Allah is ahad," and one does not say "Zayd is ahad," because Allah has the exclusive quality of being Ahad, whereas Zayd can have various states. End of quote. What he mentioned, that ahad does not admit what has been described, is refuted by counting.

Aban ibn 'Uthman, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Sirin, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Sammal, Abu 'Amr in the narration of Yunus, Mahbub, al-Asma'i, al-Lu'lu'i, 'Ubayd, and Harun on his authority recited: "Ahadu Allah" (without tanwin), by dropping the tanwin because it meets the definite article (lam al-ta'rif). This is found in Arabic speech, and it occurs most in poetry, such as the poet's words:

And none remembering Allah except a little,

and such as his words:

'Amr, the one who crumbled the bread for his people.

﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ is a subject and predicate. The most eloquent reading is that these are independent sentences with predicates, by way of resumption (isti'naf), as you say: "Zayd is the scholar, Zayd is the brave." It was also said that "al-Samad" is an adjective and the predicate is the sentence after it. The explanation of al-Samad was mentioned earlier in the vocabulary section. Al-Sha'bi and Yaman ibn Riyab said: He is the One who neither eats nor drinks. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: what follows explains it, which is His words ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten﴾. Al-Hasan said: al-Samad is the solid one having no hollow, and from this is the line:

A meteor of wars whose steeds never cease, grim, chewing the bit, solid.

In the book al-Tahrir there are other opinions not supported by the language. Ibn al-Anbari said: there is no disagreement among the people of language that al-Samad is the master above whom there is no one, to whom people turn in their affairs and needs. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿He neither begets﴾ because He has no kind to be homogeneous with, so that He would have a consort of His kind and they would beget; and he indicated this meaning by His words: ﴿How can He have a son when He has no consort?﴾ [al-An'am: 101].

﴿Nor is He begotten﴾ because every begotten thing is originated and a body, whereas He is eternal with no beginning to His existence, and He is not a body. ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾: it is said "kufu" (equal), read with a damma, kasra or fatha on the kaf with a sukun on the fa', and with damma on both. Hamza and Hafs read with damma on the kaf and sukun on the fa'; Hamza hamzed it, and Hafs replaced it with waw. The rest of the seven read with damma on both and hamza. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi' eased the hamza; and in a narration from Nafi' also "kufan" without hamza, transferring the hamza's vowel to the fa' and deleting the hamza. Sulayman ibn 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas read "kifa'an" with kasra on the kaf, fatha on the fa' and the long vowel, as al-Nabigha said:

Do not hurl me with a pillar that has no equal.

Al-A'lam: "la kifa'a lahu" means "la mathila lahu" (no like for Him). Makki said: Sibawayh prefers that the adverbial phrase be the predicate when it is placed first, and al-Mubarrad faulted him with this verse, because it placed the adverbial phrase first without making it the predicate. The answer is that Sibawayh did not prohibit cancelling the adverbial phrase when placed first; he only permitted it to be a predicate or not to be a predicate, and it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial (hal) from the indefinite word, which is "ahad"; since its adjective preceded it, it was put in the accusative as a hal, so the predicate according to Sibawayh's view and preference is his, and al-Mubarrad has no proof against this view. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah also parsed it as a hal.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: the eloquent Arabic is that the adverbial phrase which is incomplete and not settled be delayed and not placed first, and Sibawayh explicitly stated this in his book, so why is it placed first in the most eloquent and most grammatically correct speech? I say: this statement was only made to negate equality from the Essence of the Creator, glory be to Him, and this meaning's focus and center is this adverbial phrase, so it was the most important thing, the most pressing and most deserving of being placed first. End of quote.

This sentence is not of this type, because in ﴿and there is none comparable to Him﴾ the prepositional phrase is not complete; it is incomplete and cannot be the predicate of kana, rather it is connected to ﴿kufuwan﴾ and placed before it. The meaning is: "and no one was equal to Him," i.e. comparable to Him, so it has the sense of an object and is connected to kufuwan. It was placed before kufuwan for emphasis, because it contains the pronoun of the Creator, and the predicate was placed in the middle, although the original order is to delay it, because delaying the noun is a pause (fasila), so this was good. According to what we have established, the parsing of Makki and others that "lahu" is the predicate and "kufuwan" is a hal from "ahad" is invalid, because it is an incomplete adverbial phrase that cannot be a predicate; and by this the question of al-Zamakhshari and his answer are also invalidated.

Sibawayh was speaking only of the adverbial phrase which can be a predicate and can be a non-predicate. Sibawayh said: You say: "ma kana fiha ahadun khayran minka," "ma kana ahadun mithlaka fiha," and "laysa ahadun fiha khayrun minka," when you make "fiha" a settled element (mustaqirran) and do not make it like your saying "fiha Zayd qa'im." The adjective is applied to the noun. If you make it like "fiha Zayd qa'im," you put it in the accusative, so you say: "ma kana fiha ahadun khayran minka," and "ma kana ahadun khayran minka fiha," except that when you want cancellation (al-ilgha'), the more you delay the cancelled element the better, and when you want it to be settled (mustaqirr), the more you put it first the better; and the placing first, delaying, cancelling and settling are good, abundant Arabic. God the Exalted said: ﴿and there is none comparable to Him﴾, and the poet said:

As long as among them there is a living suckling camel.

End of quote. What we have quoted is summarized, and it is in Sibawayh's words. You see his speech and his example of the adverbial phrase which can be a predicate. The meaning of his saying "mustaqirran" is a predicate of the subject and of kana. If you say: he gave the example of the noble verse, I say: this is what caused Makki, al-Zamakhshari and others to fall into what they fell into. Sibawayh only meant that the complete adverbial phrase, in the verse "ma dama fihinna fasilun hayyan," was treated as a complement (fadla) and not a predicate, just as in the verse it was treated as a complement; so he made the adverbial phrase which can be a predicate like the incomplete adverbial phrase in not being used as a predicate. Anyone of sound mind knows that no sentence is formed from "wa lam yakun lahu ahad," rather if "kufuwan" were delayed and raised as an adjective and made its predicate, no sentence would be formed from it; rather you see that the negation applies only to the predicate, which is "kufuw," and "lahu" is connected to it, and the meaning is: "and there was not for Him anyone equal to Him." Many hadiths have come about the virtue of this surah, among them that it equals one third of the Qur'an; the scholars have spoken on this, and this is not its place. And Allah is the Granter of success.

I say: this statement was only made to negate equality from the Essence of the Creator, glory be to Him, and this meaning's focus and center is this adverbial phrase, so it was the most important thing, the most pressing and most deserving of being placed first. End of quote.

The adjective is applied to the noun. As long as among them there is a living suckling camel.

Many hadiths have come about the virtue of this surah, among them that it equals one third of the Qur'an; the scholars have spoken on this, and this is not its place. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Surah al-Ikhlas is Meccan and has four verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge.﴾ ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten.﴾ ﴿And there is none comparable to Him.﴾

Al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge): it is fa'al in the sense of maf'ul, from samada ilayhi, meaning he turned to him intending him, and he is the master to whom one turns in needs and who alone suffices for them. The poet said:

Has the messenger of ill news come in the morning with the best of the Banu Asad, with 'Amr ibn Mas'ud, the master, the Samad?

Another said:

I struck him with a sword, then I said to him: "Take it, you are disgraced, for you are the master, the Samad."

Al-kufu (the equal): the peer.

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge.﴾ ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten.﴾ ﴿And there is none comparable to Him.﴾ This surah is Meccan according to the opinion of 'Abd Allah, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, 'Ata', Mujahid and Qatadah, and Madinan according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak.

Since what preceded it mentioned the enmity of the nearest of people to the Messenger (ﷺ), namely his uncle Abu Lahab, and what he suffered from the worshippers of idols who took other gods along with Allah, this surah came expressly affirming Tawhid (the oneness of God), refuting the idol-worshippers, those who said in dualism and trinitarianism and other doctrines opposed to Tawhid. (p-528)

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Jews said: "O Muhammad, describe your Lord to us and give us His lineage," so this was revealed. And it is narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah that the leaders of the factions said: "Give us the lineage of your Lord," so this was revealed. If this cause is authentic, then the pronoun (huwa) refers to the Lord, i.e. ﴿Say: He is Allah﴾, meaning my Lord is Allah, and it is a subject and predicate, with "Ahad" as a second predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ahad" is a substitute for "Allah" or (it is) "huwa ahad." End of quote. If the cause is not authentic, then huwa is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), the matter is the subject, and the sentence after it is a subject and predicate in the position of the predicate of huwa. "Ahad" here means "wahid" (one), i.e. singular in every aspect of unity, meaning in His essence and attributes, not divisible. The hamza of this "ahad" is substituted from a waw, and substituting an open hamza for a waw is rare; from this is the phrase "imra'ah anah" meaning "wanah," because it derives from al-wany, which is weakness, just as "ahad" derives from al-wahda (unity).

Tha'lab said: there is a difference between wahid and ahad. The wahid admits counting, plurality and the dual, while the ahad does not admit them. One says "Allah is ahad," and one does not say "Zayd is ahad," because Allah has the exclusive quality of being Ahad, whereas Zayd can have various states. End of quote. What he mentioned, that ahad does not admit what has been described, is refuted by counting.

Aban ibn 'Uthman, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Sirin, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Sammal, Abu 'Amr in the narration of Yunus, Mahbub, al-Asma'i, al-Lu'lu'i, 'Ubayd, and Harun on his authority recited: "Ahadu Allah" (without tanwin), by dropping the tanwin because it meets the definite article (lam al-ta'rif). This is found in Arabic speech, and it occurs most in poetry, such as the poet's words:

And none remembering Allah except a little,

and such as his words:

'Amr, the one who crumbled the bread for his people.

﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ is a subject and predicate. The most eloquent reading is that these are independent sentences with predicates, by way of resumption (isti'naf), as you say: "Zayd is the scholar, Zayd is the brave." It was also said that "al-Samad" is an adjective and the predicate is the sentence after it. The explanation of al-Samad was mentioned earlier in the vocabulary section. Al-Sha'bi and Yaman ibn Riyab said: He is the One who neither eats nor drinks. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: what follows explains it, which is His words ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten﴾. Al-Hasan said: al-Samad is the solid one having no hollow, and from this is the line:

A meteor of wars whose steeds never cease, grim, chewing the bit, solid.

In the book al-Tahrir there are other opinions not supported by the language. Ibn al-Anbari said: there is no disagreement among the people of language that al-Samad is the master above whom there is no one, to whom people turn in their affairs and needs. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿He neither begets﴾ because He has no kind to be homogeneous with, so that He would have a consort of His kind and they would beget; and he indicated this meaning by His words: ﴿How can He have a son when He has no consort?﴾ [al-An'am: 101].

﴿Nor is He begotten﴾ because every begotten thing is originated and a body, whereas He is eternal with no beginning to His existence, and He is not a body. ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾: it is said "kufu" (equal), read with a damma, kasra or fatha on the kaf with a sukun on the fa', and with damma on both. Hamza and Hafs read with damma on the kaf and sukun on the fa'; Hamza hamzed it, and Hafs replaced it with waw. The rest of the seven read with damma on both and hamza. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi' eased the hamza; and in a narration from Nafi' also "kufan" without hamza, transferring the hamza's vowel to the fa' and deleting the hamza. Sulayman ibn 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas read "kifa'an" with kasra on the kaf, fatha on the fa' and the long vowel, as al-Nabigha said:

Do not hurl me with a pillar that has no equal.

Al-A'lam: "la kifa'a lahu" means "la mathila lahu" (no like for Him). Makki said: Sibawayh prefers that the adverbial phrase be the predicate when it is placed first, and al-Mubarrad faulted him with this verse, because it placed the adverbial phrase first without making it the predicate. The answer is that Sibawayh did not prohibit cancelling the adverbial phrase when placed first; he only permitted it to be a predicate or not to be a predicate, and it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial (hal) from the indefinite word, which is "ahad"; since its adjective preceded it, it was put in the accusative as a hal, so the predicate according to Sibawayh's view and preference is his, and al-Mubarrad has no proof against this view. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyyah also parsed it as a hal.
